newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: FEATURE-Foreigners speed recovery of Cambodia's Moslems.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Foreigners speed recovery of Cambodia's Moslems.

text.p: The haunting call to prayer floats over the onion-domed mosques and simple wooden houses of this riverside Moslem community, where a spiritual and cultural revival is under way.

Scores of men from the ethnic Cham community, young and old, pack into the brick, stucco and cement mosques for Friday prayers two decades after the ultra-nationalist and atheist Khmer Rouge destroyed their temples and killed tens of thousands of Moslems nationwide.

The scenes of healthy religious activity owe much to the generosity of overseas Moslem benefactors, motivated by religious and humanitarian concerns, who have helped speed the rebirth of a minority devastated under the brutal 1975-79 Khmer Rouge rule.

Malaysians, Indonesians and Arabs have funnelled money into the Cham community since a U.N.-brokered peace treaty was signed in 1991, ushering in a two-year peacekeeping force that numbered soldiers from several Islamic nations.
PRAYER AND EDUCATION
"Their aim is firstly to have enough mosques for Moslems to pray in and secondly to educate them to understand Islam," said Ismail Osman, adding: "They want to strengthen Islam."

The Cham official has elicited help from contacts made in Malaysia and Indonesia during years in exile. Matt Ly and Ahmad Yahya, two of the three Moslem members of Cambodia's 120-member parliament, have also won key funds for their rival Islamic agencies.
Overseas Islamic aid agencies here stress the humanitarian nature of their mandate, while acknowledging a religious angle.

Ismail Osman, a top official at the Ministry of Cults and Religion, estimated that donors in Malaysia, Indonesia and the Middle East had given $7-8 million since U.N.-run polls in 1993 restored an internationally-recognised government.

He said they had helped rebuild or construct more than 250 mosques and several schools for the Chams, who first settled in Cambodia some 500 years ago after the breakup of the central Vietnam empire of Champa.

Ahmad Yahya, a deputy for the royalist FUNCINPEC party, agreed that foreign assistance had helped revitalise the Cham community, saying: "We are moving in the right direction, but it is picking up slowly, so we need help from each (overseas Moslem) individual to develop Cambodia."
MOSLEMS RUN THEIR OWN AFFAIRS
The MP, whose Cambodian Islamic Development Association has been a conduit for channelling aid to the Chams, insisted that local Moslems were in charge of their own destiny.

But some analysts believe a price may be attached to aid and they fear the spectre of a fundamentalist crusade in this small southeast Asian nation, where the Cham population of about 400,000 accounts for less than five percent of the population.
William Collins, author of a study on the Chams, said the Arabs who fund construction of the bigger mosques might want them to purify local Islam and bring it more in line with the Middle East.
Collins told Reuters that an evangelical brand of orthodox Islam had been imported in some areas from Malaysia and the southern Thailand provinces of Yala and Pattani.
"It is gaining importance; it remains to be seen how widespread it will be," he said.
General Skadavy M. Ly Roun, a Cham and head of Cambodia's Interpol liaison office, voiced fears about the fundamentalist influences in an essentially Sunni Moslem community.
"I know there are some Shia, they used to send their people to Cambodia. Now we don't have this problem...but maybe later."

But Ahmad Yahya did not agree, saying: "Until now we have not received any finance from the governments of the Middle East and no individual has asked us in return (for aid) to follow this kind of sect or that kind of sect.
"We are Sunni Moslem...We are not like Shia," he said of the strict orthodox strain.
ARAB AID ORGANISATIONS
No Middle East nation maintains an embassy in Cambodia but there are at least three aid organisations from the Arab world.
The Saudi Om Al-Qura Organisation stresses it is here to help all Cambodians with medical care, but acknowledges it sent 10 Moslems to study religion and language in Pattani.
The Kuwait-based Revival of Islamic Heritage Society last year opened a $2 million orphanage for 400 Cham males. Staff said they taught a regular Cambodian syllabus along with religious classes.

The aid is welcome to a community devastated by the Khmer Rouge tyranny, but Ahmad Yahya says it will take up to 50 years to raise overall standards among a community that has got used to rubbing shoulders with the poorest of the poor in Cambodia.

Collins says the revival of Cham identity and culture owes much to the abuses they suffered under the Khmer Rouge, when they were targeted for their communal strength, language and religious beliefs -- many were forced to eat pork, for example.
"Many of their villages were totally laid waste. That's part of the impulse of building the mosques of brick, stucco and cement -- it's a way of saying we don't want to be moved any more."
